case_name: Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 (No. 1)
text:
Ross v. New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 (No. 1)

1990-01-30

New Brunswick Queen's Bench

CHRR Doc. 90-056

Malcolm Ross

Applicant

v.

The Board of School Trustees, District No.15, Human Rights Board of Inquiry, David Attis, Human Rights Commission, The Minister of Labour, Department of Education, New Brunswick Teachers' Federation, The Canadian Jewish Congress

Respondent

Date of Decision: January 30, 1990

Before: New Brunswick Queen's Bench, Landry J.

Appearances by: Malcolm Ross on his own behalf

Joseph E. Weir, Human Rights Commission;

Gabriel Bourgeois, Minister of Labour;

C. Clyde Spinney, The Department (Minister) of Education;

George P. Filliter, New Brunswick Teachers' Federation;

Joel Richler, The Canadian Jewish Congress.

BOARDS OF ADJUDICATION / INQUIRY — reasonable apprehension of bias — PROCEDURE — application to examine on discovery the chairperson of a board of inquiry appointed to hear complaint

Summary:
The Court of Queen's Bench dismisses an application by Malcolm Ross to examine on discovery Brian Bruce, who was appointed by the Minister of Labour of the Province of New Brunswick to hear and decide a complaint against Mr. Ross and the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15.

The complaint against Mr. Ross alleges that he and the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15. discriminated against David Attis and his children with respect to a public service because of their religion.

Malcolm Ross is a teacher in the district where David Attis's children attend school. Mr. Ross's anti-Semitic views have been widely publicized and, Mr. Attis alleges, condoned by a the School District, with the effect that his children are being schooled in a discriminatory atmosphere.

Malcolm Ross alleges in his application that there is a reasonable apprehension of bias regarding Brian Bruce and that he should be allowed to examine Mr. Bruce through a discovery process in order to gather further information regarding this bias. Mr. Ross also applies to examine on discovery the Minister of Labour and the Chief Commissioner of the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission.

The Court declines to grant the application. There is no evidence offered by Mr. Ross to support the allegation of bias with respect to Mr. Bruce. Also the Court finds that there can be no reason to examine the Minister of Labour or the Chief Commissioner of the Human Rights Commission with respect to their bias since at this point the person who will hear and decide the complaint is Brian Bruce.

The application is dismissed.

Legislation Cited

New Brunswick

Rules of Court,
N.B. Reg. 82-73:  2

Landry J. (Orally)

[
1
]    In his motion, the applicant requests, first, an order that the examination of the three respondents mentioned in his written motion dated January 17, 1990 be allowed to proceed as the three refused to appear on January 25, 1990; and, second, an order setting a new date for the examination.

[
2
]    Pursuant to
Rule 32.02(1)
of the
Rules of Court
,
[N.B. Reg. 82-73], and the definition of "action" in
Rule 1.04
, only parties to an action have an automatic right to examine one another by way of examination for discovery. The applicants and respondents in an application have no such right.

[
3
]    Section 32.02(1) reads:

A party to an action may examine for discovery, once, without leave, any other party who is adverse in interest.

Rule 1.04 defines "action" as follows:

"
action
" means a proceeding commenced by issuing a Notice of Action.

[
4
]    We are dealing here, Mr. Ross, with a Notice of Application. Rule 38.09(b) reads:

On the hearing of an application, the court may . . .

(b)    where it is satisfied that there is a substantial dispute of fact, direct that the application proceed to trial or direct the trial of a particular issue or issues and, in either case, give such directions and impose such terms as may be just, subject to which the proceeding shall thereafter be treated as an action.

[
5
]    Rule 39.02(1) reads:

Prior to the hearing of a motion or application, a person who is not a party to the proceeding may be examined, cross-examined and re-examined, for the purpose of having a transcript of his evidence available for use upon the hearing thereof, and the procedure set out in Rule 33 applies.

"When there is a substantial dispute of facts," which is not the case here, it is in the discretion of the court whether to convert an application into an action, and allow for an examination for discovery of the parties.

[
6
]    We have here a situation where the applicant claims in the application proper that a board of inquiry, composed of one individual, Brian Bruce, has been established in circumstances that gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias. The applicant, it seems to me, must, as is usual in applications, provide evidence by way of affidavit to support his allegation of reasonable apprehension of bias. In the circumstances, it would not be right at all to allow the applicant to go on a fishing expedition and examine on discovery Brian Bruce, who is the board of inquiry, appointed to hear the complaint against the applicant, particularly where the affidavit submitted by the applicant contains very scant evidence relating to Brian Bruce directly. It would not be right to allow examination on discovery of Brian Bruce.

[
7
]    The applicant also wants to examine the Minister of Labour and the New Brunswick Human Rights Commissioner. I must say, firstly, that it seems to me, at this stage anyway, that the only relevant bias, if any, in this case is the bias that might exist in the board of inquiry, Brian Bruce. The allowing, in the circumstances, of examination for discovery of the Minister of Labour and the New Brunswick Human Rights Commissioner, is not warranted and would not be proper.

[
8
]    The applicant, as is usual in applications, has submitted an affidavit and other items referring to utterances by the Minister of Labour and the New Brunswick Human Rights Commissioner, and I don't think, for the reasons above, that the interest of justice would be served by allowing their examination on discovery.

[
9
]    In making this ruling, I am mindful always that the court must ensure that all relevant facts are put before it, that the procedure is fair to all parties, including the respondents as well as the applicant, and that matters are disposed of as expeditiously and efficiently as possible. For those reasons, examination will not be ordered, and the applicant's motion is dismissed.
